description: Static website bucket with a public-read ACL and an open bucket policy; server-side encryption and versioning are not configured.
Private backup bucket encrypted with a rotating KMS key, versioning enabled, lifecycle rules, and full public-access blocking.
Bastion EC2 host with a security group allowing SSH and RDP from the internet; the root volume is unencrypted and detailed monitoring is off.
Application server with encrypted EBS volumes, IMDSv2 enforced, detailed monitoring, and a security group limited to the office CIDR range.
Shared IAM user attached to AdministratorAccess with an active long-lived access key and an inline policy granting wildcard actions on all resources.
Developer IAM role scoped to specific S3 and CloudWatch actions with MFA-enforced assumption, plus a strict account password policy.
MySQL instance marked publicly accessible with unencrypted storage, a weak hardcoded master password, and automated backups disabled.
Postgres instance in private subnets with KMS-encrypted storage, seven-day backups, deletion protection, and enhanced monitoring.
Image-resize Lambda with an over-permissive execution role, no dead-letter queue or tracing, and an API key hardcoded in environment variables.
Order-processing Lambda in private subnets with a scoped execution role, dead-letter queue, active tracing, and reserved concurrency.
Kubernetes cluster with a public API endpoint open to the internet, no control-plane logging or secrets encryption, and worker nodes in public subnets.
Private-endpoint Kubernetes cluster with audit logging, KMS secrets encryption, and managed node groups in private subnets.
Three-tier VPC with public and private subnets and a NAT gateway, but VPC flow logs are not configured and a database security group allows Postgres from anywhere.
Single-region CloudTrail without log-file validation or KMS encryption, writing to a bucket with no versioning or access logging.
Multi-region CloudTrail with log-file validation and KMS encryption, but the destination bucket has no server-side encryption configured and the CloudWatch log group never expires.
Customer-managed KMS key with automatic rotation disabled and a key policy allowing any AWS principal to decrypt.
Customer-managed KMS key with yearly rotation, a 30-day deletion window, and a key policy limited to the payments service role.
Public application load balancer serving plain HTTP with no redirect to HTTPS, access logging disabled, and no deletion protection.
Application load balancer with HTTPS-only listeners on a modern TLS policy, HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect, S3 access logging, deletion protection, and an attached WAF.
Session and audit tables using default encryption with point-in-time recovery disabled and no TTL on expiring records.
Orders table encrypted with a rotating customer-managed key and TTL configured on expiring attributes, but point-in-time recovery is not enabled.
Notification pipeline with a KMS-encrypted SNS topic enforcing TLS-only publishers, but the subscribing SQS queue has no encryption and no dead-letter redrive policy.
FIFO topic with content-based deduplication and an encrypted queue, but the topic policy allows publishing from any AWS principal.
Data-tier security group exposing database ports to the internet with unrestricted egress, including a separate open MySQL ingress rule.
EC2 application host with encrypted volumes and IMDSv2, but its instance-profile role mixes a scoped S3 policy with a wildcard administrative statement; AMI resolved via data source.
Encrypted Postgres with seven-day backups and a snapshot-export role, but the export bucket uses a public-read ACL without encryption.
Fully private VPC with flow logs to CloudWatch, SSM-managed instances with encrypted volumes and IMDSv2, and a security group limited to the office range.
Serverless API with database credentials hardcoded in Lambda environment variables, a wildcard IAM policy, no VPC attachment, and no dead-letter handling.
Container registry with scan-on-push enabled but mutable tags and no lifecycle policy, paired with a staging cluster whose API endpoint is publicly reachable.
Autoscaled web tier behind a load balancer with encrypted root volumes, but instances get public IPs and the target group health check runs over plain HTTP.
Storage account permitting public blob access over TLS 1.0 with shared-key authorization and no network restrictions.
Storage account enforcing TLS 1.2, denying public blob access and shared-key auth, restricted to one virtual network, with blob versioning on.
Key vault without purge protection, open to all networks, with an access policy granting full key management to one user and a hardcoded secret value.
Key vault with Azure RBAC authorization, purge protection, default-deny network ACLs, and audit diagnostics flowing to Log Analytics.
SQL server with a firewall rule open to the whole internet, a weak SA password, TLS 1.0, and transparent data encryption disabled on the database.
SQL server with public access disabled, a generated admin password, an Azure AD administrator, TDE, and 90-day extended auditing.
Windows web app serving plain HTTP with TLS 1.0, FTP allowed, no managed identity, and a database connection string in plain app settings.
Linux web app enforcing HTTPS with minimum TLS 1.2, FTPS-only deployment, and a system-assigned managed identity.
Managed Kubernetes cluster without RBAC or network policy, a public API server, and no monitoring addon on the default node pool.
Private AKS cluster with Azure RBAC, Calico network policy, Key Vault secrets provider, monitoring, and a tainted user node pool.
Network security group with an inbound rule allowing RDP from any internet address on the workload subnet.
Segmented virtual network with a least-privilege NSG, but NSG flow logs are not configured so denied traffic goes unrecorded.
Cosmos DB account reachable from the public internet with no IP firewall and only eight hours of periodic backup retention.
Cosmos DB account restricted to the office IP range with weekly periodic backups, but without a private endpoint and using only Microsoft-managed keys.
Storage account locked to specific IPs and subnets, paired with a key vault that has soft-delete but no purge protection; firewall rules generated from variables.
HTTPS-enforced web app backed by a SQL server whose firewall allows the whole internet, with the database password in plain application settings.
Network security group exposing the SQL Server port to the internet on the data subnet.
Basic-SKU container registry with the admin account enabled, attached to an RBAC-enabled AKS cluster with a private node subnet.
Minimal key vault with soft-delete, purge protection, and default-deny network access for application secrets.
Hub virtual network with proper subnetting, but the management NSG retains a legacy rule allowing all high ports from the internet.
Storage bucket granting object viewer to allUsers with versioning disabled and no customer-managed encryption.
Storage bucket with uniform access, public-access prevention enforced, versioning, a rotating CMEK, and a lifecycle rule expiring old versions.
Two legacy VMs with external IPs, IP forwarding enabled, no shielded-VM features, and the default service account on full cloud-platform scope.
VM with shielded-VM features and OS Login enabled, but carrying a public external IP; a second instance is correctly private.
GKE cluster using legacy basic authentication with a public control plane, no network policy, and node pools on full API scopes.
Private GKE cluster on the regular release channel with workload identity, network policy, shielded nodes, and binary authorization enforced.
Postgres instance with a public IP open to all addresses, automated backups disabled, SSL not required, and a weak application password.
Postgres instance on private IP only with automated backups, point-in-time recovery, required SSL, CMEK, and deletion protection.
Project IAM granting the basic Owner role to a CI service account, Editor to a broad group, and a long-lived service-account key.
Custom IAM role scoped to logging and monitoring for an analyst, but the basic Editor role is still granted to a developer account.
VPC firewall rules allowing all protocols from the entire internet inbound and unrestricted egress to everywhere.
Firewall rules generated from a variable map with dynamic allow blocks, alongside a legacy rule still permitting TCP 8080 from anywhere.
Versioned storage bucket without CMEK paired with a shielded VM whose service account carries full cloud-platform scope; image resolved from a data source.
Private Cloud SQL with backups and point-in-time recovery backing a GKE cluster that has workload identity but node pools running on full API scopes.
VMs relying on SSH keys baked into instance metadata, with public IPs and the default service account on full scope.
Storage bucket with uniform access, versioning, and lifecycle management, but no customer-managed encryption, no access logging, and viewer access granted to an external group.
GKE node pools running with minimal service-account scopes and workload identity, but the container.admin role is granted to a broad developer group.
Auto-mode VPC with subnets lacking flow logs and a firewall rule allowing all internal traffic.
Cloud SQL with backups, required SSL, and IP restricted to the office range, but without CMEK or deletion protection.
GKE and Cloud SQL composed through a local network module with dynamic node pools; the cluster is private with workload identity, but SQL authorized networks include the whole internet.
